Parameters: threshold (dB level above which compression activates), ratio (attenuation amount above threshold, e.g. 4:1), attack time (response time to reach full compression), release time (time to return to unattenuated state), makeup gain (compensation for overall level reduction). Persistence mechanism: implemented as analog circuitry (VCA-based compressor designs like the Fairchild 670, SSL bus compressor) or digital algorithms (lookahead, oversampled, multiband variants) that execute the gain-reduction computation on each audio frame. payload.body: Frequency modulation is a technique of signal processing in which the instantaneous frequency of a higher-frequency carrier signal is varied in proportion to the amplitude of a lower-frequency modulating signal: the carrier's phase continuously accumulates the integral of the modulating signal, so the information rides on frequency variation rather than amplitude variation. For a sinusoid modulator the output contains the carrier plus sideband pairs at f_carrier ± n·f_modulator for every integer n (Bessel expansion), with occupied bandwidth given by Carson's rule, ≈ 2(Δf + f_max). Its parameters are the peak frequency deviation Δf in Hz, the modulating frequency, the modulation index Δf/f_modulator, and the carrier frequency. The persistence mechanism: analog FM realizes it in a voltage-controlled oscillator whose control input tracks the modulating signal; digital FM accumulates a per-sample phase increment in a phase accumulator and synthesizes the carrier from it; and it persists institutionally as the operating standard of FM radio broadcasting (87.5–108 MHz) and two-way and marine radio, and as a synthesis engine in audio (Chowning's FM synthesis, 1973). [formal: modulatio frequentiae | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.12]

payload.name: chorus
payload.scope: A human-made audio processing technique: duplicating a signal, applying slight pitch variation and time delay to each copy, and mixing the copies back with the original to thicken the perceived sound — built to persist as a standard effect in guitar pedals, synthesizers, and studio processing.

payload.body: Chorus is an audio processing technique that takes an input signal, creates one or more duplicates, applies a low-frequency oscillator to vary the pitch (typically ±5–20 cents) and delay time (typically 15–40 ms) of each copy, and mixes the processed copies back with the original unprocessed signal. The LFO frequencies are set lower than those in a flanger (typically 0.5–3 Hz vs 0.1–2 Hz), and the modulation depth is wider, creating a shimmering thickening effect that simulates multiple sources playing in slight unison. The technique persists as embedded circuitry in guitar pedals, DSP algorithms in studio software, and built-in patches on synthesizers. [formal: chorus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Tremolo is an audio effect that produces periodic variation in the amplitude (volume) of a sound signal, creating a pulsating or quavering effect. The mechanism uses a low-frequency oscillator (LFO) to modulate the amplitude envelope of the audio signal: the LFO generates a periodic waveform — typically sine, triangle, or square — at a rate between 0.1 Hz and 20 Hz, and the instantaneous amplitude of the audio signal is multiplied by the LFO output (normalized to 0–1 range). Parameters include rate (LFO frequency in Hz, typically 0.1–10 Hz for musical tremolo), depth or intensity (how far amplitude swings from full volume to minimum, 0–100%), and waveform shape (sine for smooth pulsation, square for on/off gating effect). The persistence mechanism: analog tremolo circuits use an LFO driving a voltage-controlled amplifier in the audio path; digital tremolo implements amplitude multiplication in DSP code or as plugin effects (VST, AU, AAX); tremolo persists as a standard feature in guitar amplifiers, stompbox pedals, synthesizers, and studio software. [formal: tremolo | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Vibrato is an audio effect that produces a slow, periodic variation in the pitch (frequency) of a sound signal, creating a wavering or throbbing quality. The mechanism uses a low-frequency oscillator — classically a sine wave at 4-8 Hz — to modulate the frequency of the sound source: in a synthesizer the LFO output is summed into the pitch input of the voltage-controlled oscillator, shifting its instantaneous frequency by the depth amount; in digital plugins the same LFO modulates the playback rate or phase accumulator of the source. Parameters: rate (LFO frequency, conventionally 4-8 Hz — slow enough to read as vibrato rather than trill or wobble), depth (peak pitch deviation, typically a few cents up to about a semitone), and waveform shape (sine for the classic smooth vibrato, triangle/square for harder character). Persistence mechanism: the pitch-LFO section of analog and digital synthesizers, vibrato circuits and effects in guitar amplifiers and pedals, DSP implementations in studio software (VST, AU, AAX plugins), and built-in effects in keyboards and vocal processors; specified in synthesis engineering documentation. Note on the name: many vintage guitar-amplifier controls labeled 'vibrato' in fact implement tremolo (periodic AMPLITUDE variation) — a historical misnomer carried over from stringed-instrument practice; this entry covers true pitch modulation, which is what the LFO definition's 'pitch (vibrato)' sense names. payload.body: A wah-wah is a human-made audio effect technique that sweeps the center frequency of a bandpass filter over time, producing a vocal-like 'wah' sound. Mechanism: the input signal passes through a bandpass filter whose center frequency is modulated by a low-frequency oscillator (LFO) or expression pedal, typically sweeping between ~200 Hz and ~2 kHz. The sweep depth, rate, and Q (bandwidth) of the filter define the effect's character. Parameters: (1) center frequency range (typically 200 Hz–2 kHz); (2) sweep rate (LFO-controlled, ~0.1–5 Hz, or expression-pedal controlled by the player); (3) filter Q (bandwidth — wider Q yields a broader, less pronounced sweep); (4) sweep depth (how far the center frequency moves). Persistence mechanism: the technique is fixed by its signal chain (bandpass filter with sweepable center frequency) and persists as hardware guitar pedals (the classic Vox wah-wah circuit), DSP plugins, synthesizer filter envelopes, and built-in patches on multi-effects units. [formal: wah-wah | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A phaser is a human-made audio effect technique that mixes a dry signal with a phase-shifted version of itself, producing a sweeping comb-filter 'swoosh' sound. Mechanism: the input signal is split into two paths — one remains dry, the other passes through a cascade of all-pass filters whose phase response creates frequency-dependent delays; the two signals are then summed, producing constructive and destructive interference (comb filtering). An LFO modulates the all-pass filter parameters, sweeping the notches through the spectrum. The result is a characteristic sweeping, swooshing sound. Parameters: (1) number of all-pass stages (typically 2–12; more stages yield deeper notches); (2) LFO rate (typically 0.01–10 Hz); (3) LFO waveform (sine, triangle, or random); (4) feedback (amount of output fed back into the all-pass chain, intensifying the notches); (5) wet/dry mix ratio. Persistence mechanism: the technique is fixed by its algorithmic recipe (all-pass filter cascade with LFO modulation, wet/dry summation) and persists as hardware guitar pedals, DSP plugins, and built-in patches on synthesizers and multi-effects units. [formal: phasor | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Law 7 asks which came first and which fed the other. Under the pinned definitions these are SIBLING modulation schemes, not ancestor and descendant: frequency-modulation varies the carrier's instantaneous frequency in proportion to the modulator's amplitude, while the ring modulator multiplies the two signals directly — product modulation, a member of the amplitude-modulation family (suppressed-carrier DSB), not a specialization of FM. The note's 'derived from the broader FM concept' inverts the hierarchy: both schemes descend from general modulation (and ring modulation from product-detection practice), and diode-ring modulators predate Chowning's FM synthesis. The note's own mechanism ('it multiplies signals') contradicts its own derivation claim. The honest edge, if any, runs from a common modulation parent, not from FM.

The accepted definition carves reverb as the TECHNIQUE creating the acoustic effect of reflections (parameters: decay, pre-delay, diffusion, damping) — implementation-neutral. The note's universal removal claim ('remove the delay-line and reverb cannot produce its characteristic density') is refuted by convolution reverb, the dominant modern class, which convolves the signal with an impulse response and contains no delay-line component at all; physical-model reverbs likewise. payload.body: Distortion is an audio effect produced by driving an electronic signal beyond the linear operating range of a circuit or algorithm, causing clipping (hard or soft) that generates new harmonic and subharmonic frequencies, thereby adding grit, warmth, or aggression to the sound. Parameters include drive/intensity (amount of overdrive), tone/equalization (post-clipping frequency shaping), and output/level (compensating for gain changes). It persists as either an analog circuit topology (tube overdrive, op-amp clipping, diode clipping) or a digital algorithm (sample-accurate waveshaping, convolution of impulse responses). The effect is foundational in electric guitar music, electronic music production, and vocal processing. [formal: distortio | substrate: matter | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Equalizer is an audio processing device or algorithm that splits an audio signal into multiple frequency bands and independently adjusts the gain (amplification or attenuation) of each band, enabling precise tonal shaping and spectral balancing of a sound source or mix. Parameters include center frequency (which frequencies are affected), bandwidth or Q factor (how narrow or wide the affected band is), and gain amount (how much the band is boosted or cut). It persists as analog hardware (rack-mounted units, mixing console sections, graphic EQ panels with fixed-band sliders) or digital software (parametric EQ plugins, FFT-based spectral processors, multiband compressors with EQ stages). Common topologies include graphic (fixed frequency bands with fixed Q), parametric (fully adjustable frequency, Q, and gain), and shelving (boosts/cuts everything above or below a frequency). Used in recording, live sound reinforcement, music production, and broadcasting. [formal: aequalizo | substrate: matter | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Noise-gate is an audio processing device or algorithm that automatically attenuates or mutes an audio signal when its amplitude falls below a user-set threshold level, thereby reducing background noise between intentional sound events. Parameters include threshold (the level at which the gate opens or closes), attack time (duration for the gate to fully open after signal exceeds threshold), hold time (minimum duration the gate remains open after signal drops below threshold), release time (duration for the gate to fully close after signal falls below threshold), and range (amount of attenuation applied when closed, from partial reduction to full mute). It persists as analog hardware (VCA-based gate circuits using voltage-controlled amplifiers) or digital software (real-time amplitude analysis with look-ahead processing). Used in recording, mixing, live sound, and broadcast to clean up microphone bleed, remove hum, and shape the decay of percussive instruments. Often combined with expanders (which provide gradual rather than binary attenuation). [formal: claustrum | substrate: matter | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.scope: A synthesizer is a human-made electronic instrument built to generate and shape sound through electronic oscillators, filters, and modulation circuits. Its persistence depends on electrical power (or battery) and user configuration of its parameters.

Its persistence depends on digital storage and a playback engine.

payload.body: A synthesizer generates sound electronically using oscillators to create waveforms, filters to shape timbre, and envelope generators to control how parameters evolve over time. Its parameters include oscillator type (sine, sawtooth, square, etc.), filter cutoff and resonance, attack/decay/sustain/release (ADSR) envelopes, and modulation destinations (LFOs routing to pitch, filter, or amplitude). It persists as an analog circuit, a digital DSP implementation, or a software plugin — all of which produce sound through controlled electronic or algorithmic oscillation rather than acoustic resonance. [formal: synthetizator | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Its parameters include sample length (how much audio is captured), play mode (one-shot, loop, or granular), pitch shifting (time-stretch or resampling), and envelope shaping (ADSR for amplitude modulation of playback). It persists as a dedicated hardware device or software plugin that stores samples in volatile or non-volatile memory and uses a real-time playback engine. [formal: sampletrum | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: Delay is a human-made audio effect technique that takes an input signal, stores it in a delay line, and returns discrete repeats of that signal at fixed or modulated time intervals, mixing the repeats back with the dry signal. Parameters: (1) delay time — the interval between the original and each repeat (typically 20 ms to 2 s; below roughly 30 ms the repeats fuse into the source and become thickening rather than discrete repeats), (2) feedback — the fraction of each repeat re-injected into the delay line, generating a geometrically decaying cascade of repeats, (3) wet/dry mix ratio — the balance between the original signal and the repeat train, (4) per-repeat filtering — a low-pass applied to each repeat damping high frequencies to simulate air absorption, (5) optional modulation — an LFO on the delay time moving the repeats chorus- or flanger-style. Mechanism: the input is stored in a delay line (tape loop, analog bucket-brigade device, or digital buffer), the stored copy is retrieved after the delay time, summed with the input, and optionally routed back through the line so each successive repeat is a scaled and filtered copy of the last. Persistence: the delay line's storage-and-retrieval is the effect's constitutive element — remove it and there is no repeat to return, and the technique reduces to plain mixing; the effect persists as embedded circuitry in guitar pedals, DSP algorithms in studio software, and built-in patches on synthesizers. [formal: delay | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.scope: A human-made audio effect technique that models the non-linear distortion and compression characteristics of magnetic tape recording, built to persist as a plugin/algorithm and hardware emulation.

payload.body: Tape saturation is an audio effect technique that simulates the non-linear harmonic distortion, soft clipping, and level-dependent compression produced when an analog magnetic tape recorder is driven beyond its linear operating range. Parameters: (1) input drive — the amount of signal pushed into the tape model, (2) saturation amount — the degree of harmonic generation and compression, (3) tape type — bias and frequency response characteristics, (4) output level — make-up gain to compensate for level loss. Mechanism: the signal passes through a non-linear transfer curve that adds even-order harmonics and progressively compresses peaks, emulating magnetic hysteresis and tape head saturation; persistence via DSP algorithms in plugins, hardware tape emulators, and documented modeling specifications. [formal: tape-saturation | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A pitch-shifter is a human-made audio processing technique and device that changes the pitch of an audio signal (its fundamental frequency and harmonic structure) while preserving its duration, in contrast to playback-speed changes that trade pitch for time. Parameters: (1) pitch interval — the transposition ratio, expressed in semitones or a continuous frequency multiplier r applied without altering playback time; (2) the duration-preservation constraint — the output timeline stays aligned to the input timeline, which is the carve separating pitch-shifting from varispeed; (3) time-alignment mechanism — PSOLA/WSOLA pitch marking and time realignment, phase-vocoder spectral interpolation, granular segmentation and re-synthesis, or resampling with time correction; (4) artifact behavior — phase smearing and granularity as a function of shift magnitude. Persistence mechanism: hardware pedals and rack units, software plugins in standardized formats (VST, AU, AAX), and DSP algorithms embedded in DAWs and synthesizers, transmitted through music-production practice. [formal: mutatio toni | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.note: Remove-Y test: jitter is defined as measurable variation of sample/frame timing relative to their EXPECTED positions. Those expected positions (n·1/fs, the ideal grid) exist only because the sample clock stamps each sample position with a defined interval. Remove the sample clock — no periodic timing reference — and there is no sample position, no ideal grid, hence no expected position to deviate from: the construct loses its measuring reference and stops operating. The reverse does not hold: the clock needs no jitter; jitter is a property measured against the clock, not the clock against jitter. (The cluster's earlier target 'clock' carved a PUBLIC timekeeping device; this is the machine-internal grid the definition actually measures against.)

payload.body: A sample-clock is a human-made timing reference that establishes a periodic grid marking the position of every audio sample in digital audio. It persists as a fixed sampling rate (e.g., 44.1 kHz, 48 kHz, 96 kHz) — the number of samples per second — which all digital audio hardware and software must agree on for correct playback and recording. Parameters: (1) sampling rate — the periodicity of the clock, expressed in samples per second; (2) clock source — the physical oscillator, crystal, or PLL that generates the timing pulses; (3) word length — the bit depth defining quantization, independent of but synchronized to the sample-clock. The mechanism of persistence: the sampling rate is encoded in audio file formats (WAV, AIFF, FLAC), specified in hardware specifications (audio interfaces, DACs, ADCs), and enforced by DSP implementations that process exactly N samples per second. payload.body: A phase-locked loop is a human-made feedback control system that locks the phase and frequency of an internally generated signal to those of a reference input signal. It comprises three functional stages: (1) a phase detector (or phase/frequency discriminator) that compares the reference with the generated signal and outputs an error proportional to their phase difference; (2) a loop filter (low-pass) that smooths the error and sets the loop dynamics; (3) a voltage-controlled oscillator whose frequency is driven by the filtered error, closing the loop so the generated signal tracks the reference in phase and frequency. Parameters: (1) reference frequency — the frequency of the input to be tracked; (2) loop bandwidth — the range over which the loop corrects, set by the loop filter, trading tracking speed against noise rejection; (3) lock range — the band of reference frequencies over which the loop holds lock; (4) capture (pull-in) range — the band of initial frequency offsets from which the loop acquires lock. Mechanism of persistence: it persists as an engineering kind — specified in datasheets and design references (discrete PLL chips and software PLLs), fabricated as integrated circuits for frequency synthesis, clock recovery, and sample-rate conversion, and re-implemented digitally in DSP as a phase accumulator, digital loop filter, and numerically controlled oscillator; every synthesizer, receiver, and digital audio interface that derives a clock from a reference instantiates this one construct. A phase-locked loop is a human-made feedback control system that locks the phase and frequency of an internally generated signal to those of a reference input signal. It comprises three functional stages: (1) a phase detector (or phase/frequency discriminator) that compares the reference with the generated signal and outputs an error proportional to their phase difference; (2) a loop filter (low-pass) that smooths the error and sets the loop dynamics; (3) a voltage-controlled oscillator whose frequency is driven by the filtered error, closing the loop so the generated signal tracks the reference in phase and frequency. Parameters: (1) reference frequency — the frequency of the input to be tracked; (2) loop bandwidth — the range over which the loop corrects, set by the loop filter, trading tracking speed against noise rejection; (3) lock range — the band of reference frequencies over which the loop holds lock; (4) capture (pull-in) range — the band of initial frequency offsets from which the loop acquires lock. Mechanism of persistence: it persists as an engineering kind — specified in datasheets and design references (discrete PLL chips and software PLLs), fabricated as integrated circuits for frequency synthesis, clock recovery, and sample-rate conversion, and re-implemented digitally in DSP as a phase accumulator, digital loop filter, and numerically controlled oscillator; every synthesizer, receiver, and digital audio interface that derives a clock from a reference instantiates this one construct.
